paragraphs.source_en: Clarifying what your life is about through a mission statement can dramatically impact your life. As a child, Elizabeth Marks dreamed of serving in the military and enlisted at seventeen. She suffered serious injury during a deployment to Iraq, and her greatest fear was a medical discharge from the army. Sergeant Marks wrote her personal mission, “Fit for Duty,” on a piece of paper and carried it with her throughout her grueling recovery. Eventually, she became a record-breaking paraswimmer, joined the U. S. Army World Class Athlete Program, and was declared fit for duty in July 2012. II

paragraphs.source_en: When I was a teenager, I remember my dad calling a family meeting. “All right, children!” he pronounced. “We’re going to write our family mission statement!” A lot of moaning and groaning ensued. Undaunted, he continued, “The idea is to create our own family constitution. I would like everyone’s input.”

paragraphs.source_en: When it was my turn, I sarcastically said, “I think it should say, *We’re one heck of a family, and we kick butt.*” It didn’t make the final cut. But we did meet as a family several more times to refine a mission statement that said something like “Our home is a place of fun, relaxation, learning, friends, growth, and order, to develop ourselves into the kinds of people who can contribute to the world.”
